newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai parliament begins heated debate on 1998 budget.
newsitem.headline: Thai parliament begins heated debate on 1998 budget.

text.p: Thailand's parliament began a heated debate on the fiscal 1998 budget on Wednesday, with opposition leaders challenging the government's ability to balance its books in the face of a chronic economic crisis.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh kicked off a scheduled three-day debate in the elected lower house, where his six-party coalition controls 222 of 393 seats in the legislature.

"The economic slowdown has made it very tough for the government to propose a (balanced, deficit-free) budget... I believe the (1997/1998) austerity budget is appropriate under current...bearish financial sector conditions in the country," he told parliament.
Thailand's most serious economic crisis in over a decade has drastically cut government tax revenue and forced the government to slash spending plans for next year by 26.59 billion baht ($1 billion).

The country is expected to post a hefty budget shortfall of over 60 billion baht in fiscal 1997, its first deficit in a decade. The government maintains it will balance the books again in fiscal 1998 by seeking more revenue from state institutions.

Opposition leader Chuan Leekpai of the Democrat Party questioned official assertions that there will be enough tax revenue to finance the planned 982-billion-baht ($39.3-billion) expenditure next year.
"The expected tax revenue figures look suspicious...and I don't want to see a bogus balanced budget," he told parliament.

The austerity budget for fiscal 1998, which runs from October to September, boosts government spending by a modest four percent from an estimated 944 billion baht in 1996/1997. This is the smallest year-on-year spending rise in more than 10 years.

New Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya, who took office on Monday, told reporters before the debate that he would clarify government plans to seek more revenue contributions from state enterprises next year.
As the discussion started, Chavalit said his government expected the ailing economy to show signs of recovery in 1998, with improvements in the pace of growth, the current account and inflation.
Chavalit predicted Gross Domestic Product would expand by 5.7 percent from an anticipated 5.6 percent this year -- the lowest in over a decade and significantly down on the 6.4 percent rise in 1996.

He saw inflation easing to 4.4 percent in 1998 from an expected 4.5 percent in 1997. The current account deficit as a percentage of GDP would shrink to 5.3 percent in 1998 versus 6.5 percent seen in 1997.
The debate comes a day after the government issued four urgent decrees to avert a crisis in its cash-strapped finance and property sectors.
The executive decrees, which became binding immediately, sought to allow greater foreign equity participation in new banks and merging finance firms.
They also dealt with securitisation of billions of dollars in finance firm loans to the troubled property sector.

Problems in the two ailing sectors have triggered a stock market plunge to eight year lows and worsened problems caused by sluggish exports, sharply slowing economic growth and speculative attacks on the baht.
